listeningParts.title: Booking an underground mine tour
listeningParts.contextDescription: A man phones a heritage centre to book a family visit to a historic tin mine.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Polgarrow Heritage Mine, this is Jenna speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hello. We're visiting the area next month, and my wife and I would like to bring our children on one of your underground tours. Could you tell me a bit about them?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. We run two tours. The first is the Surface Trail, which is a guided walk around the old engine houses and the buildings where the tin ore was crushed. It takes about an hour, and it's all outdoors. The second is the Deep Level Tour, where you put on protective equipment and walk through the tunnels the miners dug about two hundred years ago. That one lasts about ninety minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The underground one sounds like the one the kids would really enjoy. Is there a minimum age?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There is. On the Surface Trail anyone's welcome, but for the Deep Level Tour children have to be at least seven years old. We used to take five-year-olds, but some of the passages are quite narrow and low, and younger children found it frightening, so we changed the rule last year. How old are your children?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We've got three, and the youngest has just turned eight, so that's fine.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. So that's two adults and three children. Which day were you thinking of?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We were hoping for Saturday the twelfth.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Let me check. I'm sorry, the twelfth is fully booked. Saturdays are always busy in the summer. I could offer you Sunday the thirteenth, or the following Saturday, the nineteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We're leaving on the eighteenth, so it'll have to be the Sunday. The thirteenth, then.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: No problem. On Sundays, the tours run at ten o'clock, half past twelve and three o'clock. The ten o'clock one is full, I'm afraid, so would half past twelve suit you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Half past twelve is perfect. And how much will it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: For the Deep Level Tour, it's sixteen pounds for an adult and ten for a child, but for a family of five we do a family ticket, which works out cheaper. That's fifty-four pounds for the whole group.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great, we'll take the family ticket. Is there anything we need to bring?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: We provide a hard hat with a lamp attached, and a waterproof cape, because water drips from the roof in some of the tunnels. It's eleven degrees underground all year round, even in August, so please bring a warm jumper for everyone. And you'll need shoes with a good grip, because the floor can be slippery.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's useful to know. Is there anything else for the children to do after the tour?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, they usually love the gem panning. They get a bag of sand and gravel, wash it in a stream channel, and keep any small stones they find, such as amethyst or quartz. It costs three pounds a bag, and you pay on the day.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: They'll definitely want to do that. Can I book now?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Certainly. Could I have your surname, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Delaney. D-E-L-A-N-E-Y.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you, Mr Delaney. And a contact number?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My mobile is 07946 318 520.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. When you arrive, please don't use the main car park next to the gift shop, because that's for coaches. Use the lower car park, just past the entrance gate on the left. It's free, and it's only a two-minute walk to the ticket office.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And should we arrive early?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Please arrive at least twenty minutes before your tour, so there's time to collect your equipment and watch a short safety film. If you're late, we can't let you join the group once it has gone underground.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Understood. One more question. Is there somewhere to eat?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There's a café in the old count house, where the mine managers used to work. It's famous for its pasties, which were the traditional lunch of the miners here. It does get busy at lunchtime, though, so you might want to eat before your tour.

listeningParts.title: A visit to a coal mining museum
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide welcomes a group of visitors to a museum on the site of a former coal mine.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Ashworth Colliery Museum. My name's Graham, and before you start exploring, I'd like to give you a short introduction to the site and explain what you can see in each part of the museum.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Coal was mined here for almost a hundred and fifty years, and at its busiest, in the nineteen twenties, the colliery employed over two thousand men and boys. The mine finally closed in 1991, and the museum opened five years later. Many of our volunteers are former miners, so if you see someone in a blue jacket, do ask them about their working lives. They tell the story far better than any display.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Let me say a word about why the museum looks the way it does. When the mine closed, most of the buildings were due to be demolished, and it was actually the local community, rather than the council or the coal company, that campaigned to save them. People felt that if the buildings disappeared, the history of the town would disappear with them. So the museum really belongs to the people of Ashworth.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, a few practical points. The whole site is free to enter, but there's a charge for the underground tour, which leaves from the main gate every hour. Unfortunately, the underground tour isn't suitable for wheelchair users, because the only way down is the original cage, but we have a virtual tour on a large screen in the visitor centre which shows exactly the same tunnels.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, let's look at the different buildings. The first one you'll come to is the lamp room. Before electric lamps, miners carried flame safety lamps, like the one invented by Humphry Davy in 1815. The flame was surrounded by a fine metal mesh, which stopped it from lighting the explosive gas that collects in mines. In the lamp room, you can see hundreds of lamps on the walls, and the brass tokens miners collected at the start of every shift. If a token wasn't returned at the end of the day, everyone knew that a man was still underground.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Next to the lamp room is the engine house, which contains the huge steam winding engine that raised and lowered the cage in the shaft. It's the oldest building on the site, and the engine is still in working order. We run it every Saturday afternoon, and it's well worth seeing. Please don't climb on the railings, though, as the floor below is a long way down.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Across the yard are the pithead baths. Surprisingly, until the nineteen thirties, miners here went home covered in coal dust, and they washed in a tin bath in front of the fire. The baths changed that. Today, the building holds our exhibition on the lives of mining families, including the role of women, who ran the homes and, during strikes, organised kitchens to feed the whole community. There's also a children's activity area in this building, with dressing-up clothes and a model mine.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, at the far end of the site are the stables. Ponies worked underground here, pulling wagons of coal, and some of them stayed below ground for most of the year. People are often surprised to learn that the miners became very attached to them, and the ponies were usually well cared for. Today, the stables are home to two retired ponies, Duke and Bramble, and children can help to feed them at eleven o'clock and three o'clock.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: In the same building, you'll find the display about canaries. Miners took them underground because the birds react to poisonous gas much more quickly than people do. If the canary became ill, the men knew they had to get out. British mines only stopped using canaries in 1986, when electronic detectors replaced them.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The café is in the visitor centre, and the gift shop sells books written by local people about the mine. Enjoy your visit.

listeningParts.title: A project on responsible gemstone sourcing
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two business students, Maya and Tom, discuss their research on the jewellery supply chain with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, Maya, Tom, you've chosen to look at how jewellery companies make sure their gemstones are sourced responsibly. How far have you got?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: We've done most of the background reading, and we've interviewed managers at three jewellery retailers. The main thing we've learned is that the supply chain for gemstones is much longer and more complicated than we'd imagined. A sapphire might be mined in one country, cut and polished in another, set in a ring somewhere else, and pass through several traders before it reaches a shop.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: And at every stage, information can get lost. One manager told us that by the time a stone arrives at their head office, they often only know which dealer they bought it from, not the mine where it came out of the ground.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Did you look at the Kimberley Process?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Yes, we've got a section on it. It's the international certification scheme for rough diamonds that started in 2003, after the wars in countries like Sierra Leone, where the sale of diamonds was paying for armed groups. Every shipment of rough diamonds between member countries has to have a certificate saying it's conflict-free.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: But the criticism we found most convincing is that its definition of a conflict diamond is very narrow. It only covers diamonds that fund rebel groups fighting governments. It says nothing about diamonds mined using child labour, or where workers are treated badly by governments or companies. So a diamond can be certified even if the conditions at the mine were terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And it only covers diamonds, of course. What about coloured gemstones?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: That's actually the part of the project that interested us most. There's no equivalent scheme for rubies, sapphires or emeralds, and a large proportion of them come from artisanal miners, people working on their own or in small groups, often with very simple tools.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Some estimates put the number of people working in artisanal mining worldwide in the tens of millions. And it's not all negative. For many families in rural areas, it's the main source of income, so if jewellery companies simply refused to buy from small-scale miners, it could make poverty worse rather than better.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point. Boycotts can harm the very people they're intended to protect. So what are companies doing instead?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The retailers we spoke to described a few approaches. One of them is working directly with a cooperative of miners in East Africa, paying them a fair price and funding safety training. The other two use digital tracking, where each stone is recorded at every stage, so the customer can see its whole history.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Although, to be honest, we were a bit sceptical about the tracking. The system is only as reliable as the information people put into it at the start. If someone records a stone from one mine as coming from another, the technology can't detect that.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good, that's the kind of critical thinking I want to see. What about the lab-grown stones? Some people argue they solve the whole problem.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: We've included them. Two of the three retailers now sell lab-grown diamonds, and they said younger customers in particular are choosing them. They're chemically identical to mined diamonds, and much cheaper. But they need a lot of electricity to produce, so their environmental impact depends on where the power comes from.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Right. Now, for the next stage, I'd like you to add a customer perspective. You could run a short survey asking whether people would pay more for a traceable stone.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We were thinking about that. We could do it at the university's careers fair next week, as there'll be lots of people around.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Fine, but remember that students aren't typical jewellery buyers, so mention that as a limitation. And please send me a draft of your questions by Friday, so I can check them before you start.

listeningParts.title: Lithium: the metal behind the battery
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an earth resources course on where lithium comes from and how it is produced.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today we're turning to a metal that, until quite recently, most people had never thought about, but which is now at the centre of the global shift towards electric vehicles and renewable energy. I'm talking, of course, about lithium.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's start with some basic chemistry. Lithium was identified in 1817 by the Swedish chemist Johan August Arfwedson, who found it while analysing a mineral called petalite. It's the lightest of all metals, and it's so reactive that in the laboratory it has to be stored in oil to stop it reacting with air and moisture. Its lightness, and the ease with which it gives up electrons, are exactly what make it so valuable in rechargeable batteries.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For most of the twentieth century, lithium had fairly modest uses. It was added to glass and ceramics to make them more resistant to heat, and to grease used in engines and machinery. It also has an important medical use: lithium salts have been used since the middle of the century to treat bipolar disorder. But today, the majority of lithium produced goes into batteries, and demand has grown enormously.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So where does it come from? There are two main sources. The first is brine, which is very salty water found beneath salt flats in dry, high-altitude regions. The best-known area is the so-called lithium triangle, where Chile, Argentina and Bolivia meet, which is thought to hold more than half of the world's known lithium resources. Here, the brine is pumped up from underground into huge shallow ponds, and the sun does most of the work. As the water evaporates, the brine becomes more and more concentrated. This takes a long time, often more than a year, and then the concentrated liquid is processed into lithium carbonate.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: This method is relatively cheap, but it's controversial. The Atacama region in Chile is one of the driest places on Earth, and local Indigenous communities have raised concerns that pumping brine, along with the fresh water used in processing, may be lowering water levels and harming the lagoons where flamingos feed. The scientific evidence is still being debated, but it's clearly an issue that companies can't ignore.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The second source is hard rock. Here, lithium is extracted from minerals, mainly one called spodumene, which is dug out of open-pit mines. Australia is the world's largest producer by this method, and it has also been the world's largest producer of lithium overall in recent years. The rock is crushed and heated to very high temperatures, and much of it has traditionally been shipped to China for refining. Hard-rock mining is faster than evaporation, but it uses more energy and produces more carbon emissions.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Because of these drawbacks, researchers and companies are investing in what's called direct lithium extraction. Instead of waiting for the sun to evaporate the water, these technologies use special filters or chemicals to pull the lithium out of the brine in hours or days, and then the remaining water can be returned underground. Several projects are also testing whether lithium can be recovered from the hot, salty water used in geothermal power plants, for example in California and in Cornwall in south-west England, where the hot springs deep underground turn out to be rich in lithium.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, there's recycling. At the moment, only a small proportion of lithium from used batteries is recovered, partly because batteries are complex and difficult to take apart safely. But as the first generation of electric cars reaches the end of its life, the amount of material available for recycling will increase dramatically, and many experts believe that recycled lithium could eventually meet a significant share of demand. In the next session, we'll look at another battery metal, cobalt, and the ethical questions surrounding its supply.

readingPassages.title: From treasure to tin foil: the story of aluminium
paragraphs: Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust, making up about eight per cent of it by weight. It is found in clays, in many common rocks and in the soil beneath our feet. Yet for most of human history it was completely unknown as a metal. The reason is chemical: aluminium bonds so strongly with oxygen that it never occurs naturally in pure form, and separating the two proved extraordinarily difficult. As a result, a metal that is now used to wrap sandwiches was, for a few decades in the nineteenth century, more valuable than gold.

The first person to produce aluminium was the Danish physicist Hans Christian Ørsted, who in 1825 obtained a tiny lump of the impure metal. Two years later, the German chemist Friedrich Wöhler improved the method, but the quantities remained minute. In 1854, the French chemist Henri Sainte-Claire Deville developed a process that used sodium to release the metal, and for the first time aluminium could be made in bars rather than grains. Even so, it remained so costly that it was treated as a luxury material, and bars of it were displayed to the public at the Paris Exhibition of 1855.

Deville's work was supported by the French emperor Napoleon III, who hoped that the light metal might be used to equip his army. According to a popular story, he also served his most honoured guests with aluminium cutlery, while less important visitors had to make do with gold. Whether or not this is exactly true, it captures how the metal was regarded. In the United States, the Washington Monument, completed in 1884, was capped with a small aluminium pyramid weighing less than three kilograms, chosen partly because the metal was so rare and admired.

The transformation came two years later. In 1886, two young scientists working on opposite sides of the Atlantic, the American Charles Martin Hall and the Frenchman Paul Héroult, independently discovered that aluminium could be produced by passing an electric current through alumina, a compound of aluminium and oxygen, dissolved in a molten mineral called cryolite. By a remarkable coincidence, both men were born in 1863 and both died in 1914. Their method, now known as the Hall–Héroult process, is still the basis of almost all aluminium production today. Hall went on to help found the company that later became Alcoa, one of the world's largest aluminium producers.

A second breakthrough soon followed. In 1888, the Austrian chemist Carl Josef Bayer patented a method for refining bauxite, a reddish rock rich in aluminium, into pure alumina. Bauxite takes its name from the village of Les Baux in southern France, where it was first identified in 1821. Together, the Bayer and Hall–Héroult processes made it possible to produce aluminium on an industrial scale, and its price collapsed. Within a generation, it had gone from a curiosity for emperors to an everyday material used in pots, pans and machinery.

The new metal found its most important role in transport. When the Wright brothers made the first powered aeroplane flight in 1903, the engine they built had a crankcase made of cast aluminium, which kept it light enough to lift the aircraft. During the twentieth century, aluminium alloys became essential to aviation, and later to cars, trains and the drinks can. However, the electrolysis process requires enormous amounts of electricity, which is why aluminium smelters are often built near cheap sources of hydroelectric power, in countries such as Norway, Canada and Iceland.

Aluminium production also creates environmental problems. The Bayer process leaves behind large quantities of a caustic waste known as red mud, which is usually stored in vast reservoirs. In October 2010, the wall of one such reservoir at an alumina plant near Ajka in Hungary collapsed, releasing a flood of red mud that swept through nearby villages, killing ten people and polluting rivers as far as the Danube. The disaster led to calls for stricter regulation of waste storage across the industry.

One of aluminium's greatest advantages, however, is that it can be recycled again and again without losing its quality. Recycling uses only about five per cent of the energy needed to produce new metal from bauxite, and the industry estimates that around three-quarters of all the aluminium ever produced is still in use. A drinks can thrown into a recycling bin today may be back on a supermarket shelf as a new can within a couple of months. For a metal once prized by emperors, it has become one of the most ordinary, and most sustainable, materials of modern life.

readingPassages.title: Messengers from the deep: how diamonds are made
paragraphs: A diamond is made of nothing more than carbon, the same element that forms the graphite in an ordinary pencil. What makes the two so different is the way their atoms are arranged. In graphite, carbon atoms form flat sheets that slide easily over one another, which is why pencil marks rub off on paper. In diamond, every atom is locked to four neighbours in a rigid three-dimensional framework, producing the hardest natural material known. On the scale of mineral hardness devised by the German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs in 1812, diamond is placed at the top, with a value of ten.

Such a structure can only form under extreme conditions. Most natural diamonds crystallised in the Earth's mantle, roughly 150 to 200 kilometres below the surface, where temperatures exceed 1,000 degrees Celsius and the pressure is tens of thousands of times greater than at sea level. These conditions are found mainly beneath the oldest and thickest parts of the continents. Dating of the tiny mineral grains trapped inside diamonds shows that many of them are extremely old, typically between one and three and a half billion years, which means that most diamonds were already ancient before the first animals appeared.

How, then, do diamonds reach the surface? The answer lies in a rare kind of volcanic eruption. Deep in the mantle, molten rock rich in gas occasionally forces its way upwards at great speed, carrying fragments of the surrounding rock, including any diamonds, with it. The speed is crucial: if diamonds rose slowly, the falling pressure would allow them to turn into graphite. The rock that fills the carrot-shaped pipes left by these eruptions is called kimberlite, and no such eruption has ever been witnessed by human beings.

Kimberlite takes its name from the town of Kimberley in South Africa, the site of one of the most famous mineral rushes in history. In 1867, a boy found a shiny pebble on a farm near the Orange River, which turned out to be a large diamond. Further discoveries followed, and from 1871 thousands of prospectors arrived to dig on a small hill. Working with picks and shovels, they created what became known as the Big Hole, more than two hundred metres deep. By the time mining stopped in 1914, it had produced nearly three tonnes of diamonds.

Not all diamonds, however, are dug from kimberlite pipes. Over millions of years, erosion wears away the rock at the surface, and rivers carry the released diamonds downstream. Because diamonds are hard and dense, they survive this journey and collect in gravels along riverbeds and coasts. Such deposits, known as alluvial deposits, were the source of the first diamonds ever mined, in India more than two thousand years ago. Today, some of the richest are found off the coast of Namibia, where diamonds carried by the Orange River to the Atlantic are recovered from the seabed by specially equipped ships.

For scientists, diamonds are valuable for a reason that has nothing to do with jewellery. Because they are so strong and chemically stable, they act as tiny time capsules, preserving fragments of minerals from parts of the Earth that can never be sampled directly. In 2014, researchers studying a small, worthless-looking diamond from Brazil reported that it contained a mineral called ringwoodite, which forms only at depths of more than 500 kilometres. The ringwoodite contained water, suggesting that this deep layer of the mantle may hold a very large quantity of water locked inside its minerals.

Impurities also give diamonds their colours. A completely pure diamond is colourless, but such stones are rare. Small amounts of nitrogen, the most common impurity, give many diamonds a yellowish tint, while traces of boron produce a blue colour. The famous Hope Diamond, now in the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, owes its deep blue colour to boron. Other colours, such as pink and red, are thought to result from distortions in the crystal structure rather than from foreign atoms, and these stones are among the most expensive in the world.

Since the twentieth century, diamonds have also been made in laboratories. In 1954, scientists at the American company General Electric produced the first reproducible synthetic diamonds by recreating the high pressures and temperatures of the mantle. A second method, developed later, grows diamonds from a carbon-rich gas, layer by layer. Synthetic diamonds were first used mainly in industry, for cutting and drilling, but gem-quality stones are now widely sold. Because they are chemically identical to natural diamonds, telling the two apart requires specialised instruments, a challenge that has transformed the work of gem-testing laboratories.

readingPassages.title: Should we mine the deep ocean floor?
paragraphs: Scattered across vast areas of the deep ocean floor, at depths of four to six kilometres, lie billions of dark, potato-sized lumps known as polymetallic nodules. They contain manganese, nickel, cobalt and copper, metals that are in growing demand for the batteries, wind turbines and power networks of a low-carbon economy. The richest known field is the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, an area of the Pacific between Hawaii and Mexico covering several million square kilometres. To mining companies, the nodules represent an opportunity to obtain these metals without the deforestation and community conflicts associated with mines on land. To many scientists, they represent one of the least understood ecosystems on the planet.

Interest in the nodules is not new. They were first brought to the surface in the 1870s by the British research ship HMS Challenger, and in the 1960s and 1970s several companies explored ways of collecting them. One of the most famous projects of that era, the ship Hughes Glomar Explorer, was publicly described as a nodule-mining vessel, but it had in fact been built for the American intelligence agency, the CIA, to secretly recover a sunken Soviet submarine. The publicity surrounding it nevertheless encouraged a belief that deep-sea mining was about to begin. It did not, largely because metal prices fell and the technical difficulties proved immense.

The legal framework was established in the decades that followed. Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the seabed beyond national jurisdiction and its mineral resources are declared the 'common heritage of mankind'. Activities there are controlled by the International Seabed Authority, based in Kingston, Jamaica, which has issued exploration contracts to governments and companies but, so far, no licences for commercial mining. In 2021, the Pacific island nation of Nauru, working with a Canadian company, triggered a rule that obliged the Authority to complete its mining regulations within two years. That deadline passed without agreement, and the negotiations have continued.

Supporters of deep-sea mining make a serious case. The world needs enormous quantities of metals to replace fossil fuels, and land-based mining has well-documented environmental and human costs, from polluted rivers to unsafe working conditions. Nodules lie loose on the seabed, so they can be collected without digging or blasting, and a single deposit can contain several valuable metals at once. In my view, these arguments deserve to be taken seriously rather than dismissed; the choice is not between mining and no mining, but between different places and methods of obtaining the materials that a cleaner energy system requires.

The difficulty is how little we know about what would be lost. A study published in 2023 estimated that around five thousand species have been recorded in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, and that the vast majority of them have not yet been formally described by science. Many animals depend on the nodules themselves, which provide one of the few hard surfaces on an otherwise soft, muddy floor. Since nodules grow by only a few millimetres every million years, removing them would eliminate that habitat for a period far longer than human history. Early tests also suggest that mining would create clouds of sediment that could smother animals far beyond the area actually mined.

The long-term evidence is sobering. In 1989, German researchers ploughed a section of the seabed off the coast of Peru to imitate the effects of mining. When scientists returned more than twenty-five years later, the plough tracks were still clearly visible, and many forms of life had not recovered. More recently, in 2024, a team led by the marine scientist Andrew Sweetman reported evidence that oxygen may be produced on the sea floor in complete darkness, possibly through electrical activity on the surface of the nodules. The finding is disputed, but it illustrates how much remains to be discovered about these environments.

Opposition has grown accordingly. A number of countries, including France and Germany, have called for a pause or a ban on deep-sea mining until its impacts are better understood. Several major companies, among them car manufacturers and technology firms, have pledged not to use metals from the seabed in their products. Meanwhile, improvements in battery chemistry have reduced the amount of cobalt and nickel needed in some designs, and better recycling could further reduce demand for newly mined metals. In my view, these developments weaken the claim that the ocean floor must be mined urgently.

Where does this leave us? It seems to me that the strongest argument is not that deep-sea mining should never happen, but that it should not begin before we understand what it would destroy. Decisions made now could cause damage lasting thousands or even millions of years, in places that belong, by international agreement, to all of humanity, including generations not yet born. Caution, in this case, is not an obstacle to progress. It is the only responsible way to make a choice that cannot be reversed.

writingTask1.title: Producing copper from ore
writingTask1.instructions: The diagram below shows the main stages in the production of copper from rock containing copper ore. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
processSteps: Rock containing copper ore is blasted and dug from an open-pit mine
Ore is carried by truck to a crusher and broken into small pieces
Crushed ore is ground with water into a fine powder
Chemicals and air are added so that copper minerals float to the surface as a concentrate
Concentrate is dried and melted in a smelter at about 1,200°C
Impure copper is cast into thick plates called anodes
Anodes are refined in tanks of acid using an electric current
Pure copper sheets (99.99%) are sold to manufacturers of wire and pipes
keyOverviewPoints: The process has eight stages, beginning with mining and ending with pure copper sheets.
It moves from mechanical stages (blasting, crushing, grinding) to chemical and high-temperature stages (flotation, smelting and electrical refining).
